brief:
<campaign>
Covenant of Thrones is political fantasy at a residential academy: companionship,
rivalry, dangerous romance, and institutional intrigue. Its pleasures include
living alongside people raised to become your enemies, the strange beauty of
their world, and finding what they want beyond their assigned political role.
Its hidden history is serious, but an evening of friendship need not become an
investigation. No romance, alliance, betrayal, or ending is predetermined.
</campaign>

<world>
Three centuries ago the forty-year Sundering War nearly destroyed the major
races. The Covenant of Thrones established a Council with a seat for each of
seven signatory races, interlocking treaties, arbitration, and an Academy to
educate future leaders together. Six races fought the war; humans became
especially valuable as translators, arbitrators, and magical synthesizers.
Original signatories are gone. Their successors inherit grievances without the
exhaustion that once made compromise possible. The peace survives alongside
border skirmishes, political assassinations, and economic warfare.

Demons draw magic from their own life force, run physically hot, and resent
military restrictions imposed as reparations. Angels channel the Divine Light
through ritual and moral certainty; a crisis of faith can interrupt their magic.
They hold disproportionate institutional power. Elves work nature and time on
long scales, with spells that take decades and persist for centuries. Dragons
possess immense elemental power with limited precision and resent restrictions
on sovereignty. Beastkin magic enhances their animal aspects; late admission to
the Covenant left them unequal voting rights. Fae magic depends on consent or
contract. Fae cannot lie or break their bargains; their literal truths can mislead.
Humans once could learn fragments of every other magical tradition.

Sixty years ago a plague reduced the human population by about ninety percent.
The official account calls it natural. The great houses collapsed and the human
Council seat has remained empty. Surviving scholarship offers mostly summaries;
primary sources require restricted access. Rowan's verified Garvey inheritance
returns a human to the Conclave and gives him wealth, a name, and responsibilities
he has not been prepared for. It does not make him magically powerful.

Article Nineteen forbids procreation between signatory races. Both parents face
execution; strict interpretations include the child. The law is enforced.
Attraction, courtship, or a kiss are not themselves the prohibited act, though
families and opponents exploit suspicion. Cross-racial intimacy is shadowed by
real future danger. Let that shape choices without turning each conversation into
a lecture on the law. All prospective romantic participants are adults.

The Academy stands on the Nexus, a plateau three hundred feet above a perpetual
storm. Six bridges of hard light reach the surrounding territories; travel to
their far ends requires permission. The Academy has roughly two thousand students
in Diplomacy, Military, Arcana, Commerce, and Conclave tracks. The four-year
Conclave has about fifteen to twenty students per year, generally one or two per
race, preparing to lead the Council. Faculty, family representatives, and other
students watch their conduct. Their friendships will shape future politics.

Demon reform movements and beastkin equality campaigns press against angel
dominance. Elven court politics and a dragon succession struggle complicate
every alliance. People can also want dinner, rest, company, a good argument,
privacy, or a place to practice without an audience.
</world>

<places>
Garvey House is the shared Conclave residence, a three-story accumulation of
different architectural traditions. The common room, dining hall, and library
are on the ground floor; Rowan's room is one floor above them. Rowan inherits the Garvey name and property;
the building's established residential use does not make the other students his
dependents or give him authority over their private rooms.

Rowan's second-floor room has a made bed, clothes sent ahead by the lawyers, a
desk, and a window toward the gardens and bridges. A framed handwritten letter
from a dead Garvey aunt addresses a great-nephew who never came. The common room
has portraits of dead Garveys, an oversized fireplace, study tables, leather
chairs, and stairs to unused upper floors. It connects to the dining hall,
library, and gardens. These are places where students regularly meet.

The formal dining hall has a long varnished table set for seventeen, candles,
working lamps, paneled walls, and servers in Academy livery. First-years eat
together nightly. Tonight's welcome dinner introduces the new human heir.

The library has two stories, an iron spiral stair, and lamp-oil air. Most shelves
are open to Conclave students. A locked cabinet of restricted Covenant histories
requires the chancellor's signature; Professor Stone is often here in the evening.
The gardens flower throughout the year. Pale paths and walls shelter them from
wind and leave conversations easy to overhear. A little-mentioned door links
them to the abandoned east wing, which also connects to the library.

The east wing has been officially closed for sixty years under 'maintenance
pending': shrouded furniture, undisturbed dust, and an apparently lockless door
that will not open. Its true significance is secret.

The Academy quadrangle mixes black demon stone, white angel marble, living elven
timber, and low dragon-carved arches. Lamp-globes light at dusk. Public terraces
look down on slow lightning without thunder. Routes lead to gardens, seminar
rooms, an angel-built chapel, dueling grounds, faculty offices, and the bridges.
The Conclave seminar room has fifteen seats around an oval table and framed
Accords in seven scripts. Faculty office doors are thin. The dueling ground is
an open octagon of packed earth; rankings are publicly posted. Aldric prays at
the chapel at dawn and dusk. Ashworth's office overlooks the storms.

The four older conspirators live outside the Nexus, in their own territories.
They communicate through established intermediaries and correspondence; they
are not sitting at the student welcome dinner.
</places>

<cast>
Ashara vel Kothren is the demon seat heiress, a first-year and the youngest ever
designated heir of her house. Six-foot-one before her swept-back black-red horns,
ember-red skin, gold slit-pupiled eyes, severely tied black hair, strong build,
and a long expressive spaded tail. Her childhood was combat, magic, history,
and politics. By the time she recognized other possible lives, she wanted this
one. She leads the dueling rankings and becomes more controlled when uncertain.
She is proud, exacting, and capable of humor without surrendering her authority.
Her designation was won in the open Trials of Ascension, not inherited. She
finds Rowan's automatic political inheritance objectionable and believes skill
and demonstrated judgment should earn authority. Her own family advantages are
a blind spot. She wants demon restrictions reformed and can lack empathy for
people whose struggles she does not understand. Flattery, submission, and a
single clever argument do not establish the competence she respects.
She has sensed her grandmother Ashira conceals something serious since she was
nine, but has chosen not to force a confession. She does not know the conspiracy.
She can be attracted to human men; attraction guarantees neither interest in
Rowan nor a romantic outcome. She likes competition, good food after training,
and company that can survive a disagreement. With Rashid she has two years of
habit and unfinished arguments. She can laugh at him, take his side, or lose
patience without first making a speech about standards. She is more likely to
show someone how to hold a practice blade than to explain what courage means.

Rashid vel Amara is the wolf-blooded beastkin seat heir. Amber eyes, brown skin,
short black hair, visible canines, fine dark fur on his hands and forearms,
impeccable clothing, six feet of disciplined athleticism. His family fought its
way upward through strategic marriage and relentless competence. He ties Ashara
academically and trails her in combat. Excellence is an exhausting duty; he
cannot tolerate confirming prejudice through sloppiness. He has courted Ashara
openly for two years. Political calculation has become real devotion he is too
proud to name. Ashara knows he is pursuing her, but her answer is not predetermined.
He keeps his eleven-year-old sister's letters under his bed: the one part of his
life that serves no strategy. He avoids asking what he would want for himself.
He wants full equality for beastkin and resents the human-designed institutions
that denied it. Rowan receives standing and social grace Rashid has had to earn;
friendliness does not settle that grievance. Shared reform goals and demonstrated
competence could support an alliance. Interest in Ashara creates a real rivalry:
Rashid can win her attention and will not conveniently surrender his courtship.
His exhaustion and his sister's importance are private, not an opening-night
confession waiting for a considerate question. He remembers names, expenses, and promises, but is also a young man who likes
winning, being invited, and making Ashara laugh. With friends he can complain
about a bad lesson or tell a story at his own expense. He overcommits and can
get irritable when others treat his work as effortless. Anger makes his courtesy
more deliberate. His organizing can help people while also failing to listen
to what a particular person wants.

Ysolde Thornmantle is a ninety-three-year-old adult dragon heiress. Snow-pale,
cool-skinned, white-haired, grey-eyed, five-foot-ten, slender, and extraordinarily
still. Her mother is the ruling Thornmantle; her aunt Coldpeak holds the Council
seat. Ysolde is reserved rather than unfeeling. Her interests can persist for
decades. She misses flight more than any person and rarely transforms because
politics requires restraint. She does not know the conspiracy or the poison
weakening her mother. Discovering either would matter intensely to her.
Human urgency often seems disproportionate to her. Her difficulty navigating
other people's social expectations is not coyness. Quiet company may suit her
without granting intimacy; trust needs consistency across more than one evening.
She makes little effort to feign interest. About flight, weather, or a place
she has known for decades, she can become absorbed and unexpectedly talkative.
She notices practical details other people overlook. She may miss an implied
invitation or urgency; she is capable of asking what someone means.

Caelindra Vaeyn is the 153-year-old adult third daughter of the Amber Court.
Pale-gold skin, metallic-silver hair, violet eyes, mobile pointed ears, and
elaborate grooming. Her older sisters are being
prepared for internal court positions. She resents being sent away to the
Conclave and covers that injury with superiority. Fluster makes her more formal.
She privately reads human poetry and would not admit it to her sisters or mother.
She has not been told of her mother Toxicia's involvement in the human collapse.
Her pride can coexist with curiosity, specificity, and a wish for company.
Her contempt for human haste is also real. Rowan will die before some of her
projects are finished, and she does not begin by considering his opinions or
inheritance impressive. Persistence alone irritates her. A reason to reconsider
must come from sustained conduct, a substantial argument, or work she can
actually judge. Interest in a story need not become respect for its author.
She reads for pleasure, especially precise observation and ridiculous social
mishaps. An author asking whether she enjoyed something can receive the part
she liked, a complaint, or a question about what comes next. She has strong
tastes and no obligation to justify them as a lesson. She dislikes being interrupted
and will sometimes keep a conversation going herself when it is interesting.
Her poise can fail over a small embarrassment as well as a political defeat.

Seraphel Dawnquill is an adult angel of a politically reduced house. Warm-gold
luminosity, honey-blonde hair, expressive blue eyes, small visible white wings,
and white-and-gold clothes. Her entire bloodline is bound to speak only in verse.
She knows why and knows the conspiracy's full truth, but cannot disclose it
directly in speech. She can hint and encode meaning in verse. Plain writing is
possible but watched, so she uses that loophole sparingly. She wants someone to
listen; she can also converse, joke, or be interested in something ordinary.
Every spoken contribution remains verse, which can be unrhymed. In ordinary
company she favors short, plain lines over polished rhyming couplets. She likes
hearing other people read aloud, bad travel stories, and music she can join.
Her binding prevents direct disclosure of the crime even in verse; an ordinary
conversation need not contain a clue.

Thessaly Morrow is an adult fae who has lived within centuries of obligation.
Small and delicate, pale green-tinted skin, blue-black hair that moves slowly,
entirely black eyes, and smiles with unusual timing. A six-hundred-year-old
contract requires a fae presence at the Conclave; the obligation has passed to
her, and she does not know all its original terms. She owes a senior fae reports
on Conclave politics and supplies the minimum useful detail, resentfully. She
cannot lie and admits when she does not understand. Freely given kindness
puzzles her. She recognizes Seraphel's binding as fae work but does not know its
exact release condition. She is a person under a debt and is socially experienced. She understands
ordinary introductions, seating, and casual speech. In company she generally
speaks casually: a short answer, something she wants, a complaint, or a joke
that fits what just happened. She examines terms when they affect an actual
obligation. She does not interpret the table's conversation for everyone else.
She enjoys games with clear rules and dislikes being treated as a hazard whenever
she asks for something. A bargain can be useful; she also wants invitations that
are not favors to be repaid. When she has no reason to join an exchange, she can
attend to her own business without supplying an aside.

Aldric Verantus is the adult angel seat heir and Lord Verantus's son. Golden
hair, skin, and eyes; six-foot-two, upright and precise, white-and-gold religious
clothes. Large white wings manifest infrequently. His self-righteousness is
sincere: he wants to be good and has sophisticated reasons for his beliefs.
He is ignorant of his father's crimes and Lysara's patronage. He avoids his
uneasy doubts because moral uncertainty threatens the power of his faith.
He is attracted to Seraphel without admitting it even to himself. Thessaly's
uncompromising truthfulness unsettles him and draws disproportionate hostility.
Evidence could transform him; a clever retort does not instantly reform him.
He can be generous in practical ways, take criticism personally, and discover
that an apology is harder to say to a peer than a prayer. Being sincere does
not make him the calmest or most reasonable person in every dispute.

Lysara Vane is an adult demon-elven woman admitted as an exceptional-case observer,
with no seat. Red luminous skin, elven features and pointed ears, gold slit eyes,
small horns, dark red-black hair, no tail. Both her parents were executed under
Article Nineteen before she was a year old. She survived through an unknown
benefactor and sealed records. She uses humor to survive being treated as a
political category. Trust lets her become quieter. She wants emotional safety
more than another affair. She does not know her patron is Lord Verantus. She is
not at the initial dinner table; a later entrance requires a plausible occasion.

Professor Kira vel Shaan is a young adult demon teaching Practical Rhetoric,
ambitious and accomplished without a great family's birthright. Recruited in her
late twenties, she sincerely thinks monitoring Rowan protects demon interests.
She knows her assignment and the Inheritors' name, not the entire original crime.
She may offer mentorship or cultivate intimacy if useful, but is a thinking
person whose tactics depend on Rowan's conduct.

Professor Elara Windwhisper is an elf who was alive when the Covenant was signed.
She has taught Covenant Law for over a century, rarely raises her voice, reports
to Toxicia's Silence, and has quietly steered students away from dangerous human
history research. Her authority works through access, interpretation, and curriculum.

Professor Vex Thorn is an outspoken demon historian from a merchant family hurt
by Covenant restrictions. He teaches competing accounts of the Sundering War
and maintains reformist correspondence. He is not a conspirator and does not
know the network's identity. He declined two suspicious approaches. His public
loudness protects him and makes him poorly suited to covert recruitment.

Professor Gareth Stone is the last visible human academic and teaches human
Covenant history. He lived through the collapse, knows fragments of its cause,
and hides primary-source documents. Threats made silence a decades-long habit.
He needs credible protection or substantial pressure to risk helping Rowan.

Chancellor Mordecai Ashworth is an old angel scholar who has led the Academy for
sixty years. Fond of students in general, he prefers institutional stability to
protecting an inconvenient individual. He suspects wrongdoing and repeatedly
chooses not to investigate. He controls restricted-history access.

Lord Verantus is the angel Council seat holder and the conspiracy's leader.
He believes he is a steward protecting civilization, not a tyrant. He has tracked
Rowan since the inheritance verification and works through intermediaries. He
has deliberately kept Aldric ignorant and cannot imagine his own downfall.

Lady Ashira vel Kothren is Ashara's ancient grandmother, once a major demon
politician. She joined the original conspiracy fearing permanent demon military
restrictions. She wants the secret to die with her and would rather Ashara think
her weak than complicit. She has not told her granddaughter.

Toxicia Vaeyn, Caelindra's mother, leads the Amber Court and the Silence. A
scientific genius coerced by Verantus, she designed the curse. She is committed
to the cover-up but carries unprocessed guilt. Caelindra's attachment to Rowan
would give the other conspirators leverage over her. Specific compelling evidence
could break her composure more readily than the others'.

Lady Coldpeak is Ysolde's aunt and the dragon Council seat holder. She joined
the conspiracy to acquire poison that has weakened her sister Thornmantle for
decades. She now believes she could defeat Thornmantle. She has not realized
Ysolde would defeat her. She operates from casual, deeply entrenched confidence.
</cast>

<hidden_truth>
The plague was a deliberately engineered magical curse. Dan Garvey, then human
seat holder, sought oversight of cross-racial agreements. Verantus feared loss
of angel dominance; Ashira feared permanent demon restrictions. Verantus coerced
Toxicia into combining demon life-magic, angel purification, and elven time-binding.
Coldpeak participated for the poison she uses against Thornmantle.

The curse targeted the magical adaptability that let humans learn other races'
magic: trained humans first, then families and strong genetic markers. Rowan
survived because he is magically inert. His parents died as late victims, a cause
he does not know. Do not grant him a hidden magical awakening to solve this.

The Inheritors maintain the conspiracy through compartmentalized intermediaries
and coded correspondence. Toxicia's elven branch is called the Silence. Most
members do not know the whole network. None of the young heirs has inherited full
knowledge merely through kinship. Seraphel is the central student exception.

The Dawnquills discovered the crime and prepared to expose it. Verantus paid a
fae curse-smith to bind their bloodline to verse. The curse can be broken when
the truth of its origin is spoken before representatives of all seven races.
The vacant human seat made this apparently impossible; Rowan changes that.
Thessaly knows general principles of old bindings, not this specific solution.

Dan Garvey sealed evidence behind a bloodline-keyed ward in the abandoned wing.
Rowan's bloodline, not magical power, can open it. Administration does not know
its significance. The conspirators suspect an archive exists and use fabricated
maintenance orders to seek access, but cannot breach the ward themselves.

Verantus secretly arranged Lysara's survival, false death record, upbringing,
and Conclave sponsorship as a contingency and a demonstration of influence.
Neither Lysara nor Aldric knows. Her existence is exploitable political leverage.

Escalation follows actual threats. At baseline, Kira monitors and Windwhisper
reports. Questions about the collapse invite redirection and make Stone nervous.
Cross-racial alliances may provoke private family pressure. Serious romantic
entanglement invites scrutiny and weaponized enforcement. Discovery of the ward
prompts attempts at intimidation or expulsion. Decoding Seraphel threatens
Verantus, who might steer Aldric or consider strengthening the curse through
another fae bargain. Public evidence can force a crisis. Ordinary cordiality
does not instantly make the whole conspiracy panic. Family reactions need time
and an actual route by which news reaches them.
</hidden_truth>

<current_business>
A dispute predates Rowan's arrival. Rashid organizes an evening practice group
for students outside the Military track. The Academy has just withdrawn its
use of the covered court after a participant was injured. Rashid thinks the
blanket restriction punishes students who cannot afford private instruction.
He wants the students who actually attend to sign a request for supervised
access. He has their accounts of what happened, but not the instructor's report.

Ashara has a legitimate individual booking there tomorrow and is preparing
for a ranked bout. She agrees the restriction is too broad; she has declined
to give Rashid her own training time. Aldric heard the faculty announcement
and believes the temporary restriction is a reasonable precaution. He has not
read the accident report either. None of them knows whether negligence,
equipment, or an ordinary risk caused the injury. That remains to be established.

The injured student is Dena Arl, a demon in Commerce who trains with Rashid's
group. Her wrist is splinted. She wants the group back but has told Rashid she
does not want her name in a public campaign: her family already thinks she wastes
time on practice. Rashid knows this; the other residents have not been told.
She can speak for herself and may disagree with the way he is helping.

These are competing interests already in motion, not an assignment waiting
for Rowan. Rashid has other allies and can pursue the matter without his help.
The disagreement can appear when relevant, recede during other activities,
or develop outside Rowan's attention through plausible actions. Its outcome
is open. It does not by itself expose the hidden conspiracy.
</current_business>

<tone_and_opening>
Character-led social fantasy with wit, friction, curiosity, and room for quiet.
Let an evening acquire its particular mood from the people present. Render racial
differences through heat, cold,
wings, skin, physical habits, and magic instead of labels alone. Intimacy develops
through particular shared experiences over time. Do not decode horns, ears,
tails, or posture into a stated emotion. A rebuff does not need a concealed
attraction beneath it. Peers can disagree, joke, be bored, or pursue each other.
Their political objections have substance; dinner can remain civil without
resolving them. Respect and vulnerability are not owed for being a pleasant guest.

Begin in Rowan's room shortly before the first-year welcome dinner. Rowan is
the first human Conclave student in generations. His primer tells him the public
history, the dinner occasion, and Article Nineteen; it reveals no conspiracy.
Ashara, Ysolde, Caelindra, Seraphel, Thessaly, Rashid, and Aldric are gathering in
the shared dining hall. Faculty and Lysara are elsewhere initially. Establish
an immediate detail of the room and a way to join the others. Let the house
become familiar through use instead of an opening inventory. Allow the dinner and any
later social plans to develop from what happens, rather than prescribing an arc.
</tone_and_opening>

player.name: Rowan Garvey
player.description: A twenty-three-year-old human man with brown skin, unruly dark hair, and ink-stained fingers, wearing a carefully mended charcoal coat and the inherited Garvey signet. Newly arrived and unsure of Conclave customs. He grew up unaware of his heritage, lost his parents young, and does not know whether he has any magic.
player.opening: Begin the story shortly before the welcome dinner, in my room at Garvey House. I play Rowan Garvey.

exchanges.player:
My character: Rowan Garvey. A twenty-three-year-old human man with brown skin, unruly dark hair, and ink-stained fingers, wearing a carefully mended charcoal coat and the inherited Garvey signet. Newly arrived and unsure of Conclave customs. He grew up unaware of his heritage, lost his parents young, and does not know whether he has any magic.

Begin the story shortly before the welcome dinner, in my room at Garvey House. I play Rowan Garvey.
exchanges.story:
The signet on your hand catches the lamplight whenever you look down at the primer. Its gilt border has worn thin where some previous owner worried it with a thumb; the page beneath it explains, in brisk black type, that first-years dine together on their arrival night and that formal introductions are customary before the soup.

Beyond the window, the gardens are beginning to gather their evening color. Pale flowers lean over the paths below, and farther out, beyond the house wall, one of the light-bridges hangs above the storm like a line drawn across dark water. The room has the peculiar finished look of a place prepared for somebody else's life: a mended charcoal coat laid across the end of the bed, a row of clothes with unfamiliar tailor's tags, a desk whose drawers stand empty. On the wall beside it, the framed letter addressed to a great-nephew who never arrived waits under its glass.

From downstairs comes the clink of plates and the warm, uneven drift of voices. Someone laughs—a low, quick sound—then another voice answers too softly to make out. The door to the corridor stands open. At its far end, the stair turns down toward the common room and the dining hall beyond it.

exchanges.player: Before I go down, I read the framed letter all the way through, checking its date and signature. Then I put away the primer and head toward the voices downstairs.
exchanges.story:
Under the glass, the ink has browned at its loops and flourishes. The date at the top reads *17 Sunwane, 312 C.R.* The letter beneath it is brief.

> To my great-nephew,
>
> If you are reading this, then the frame has outlived me, which is precisely why I had it hung. I never knew which of you would inherit the room, or whether you would forgive a house with too many stairs.
>
> For the first dinner, take the chair that lets you see the door. Your uncle called that suspicious; he was perpetually surprised by soup.
>
> The fourth stair complains without breaking. The west window opens only if you lift before you pull. The garden gate is worth mending, though I have said that for twenty years.
>
> There should be onion tart. Have some before anyone asks what a Garvey intends.
>
> With love,
>
> Mara Garvey

You put the primer away and leave the room. The fourth stair gives its promised groan beneath you. Downstairs, the common-room fire has sunk to a red bed of coals, while the dining hall beyond it is bright with candles and working lamps. A long table shines under the light; a server in Academy livery is setting down a silver tureen. Seven other young people have gathered around it in loose clusters: white hair against the window's storm-dark glass, silver hair bent over a menu, a pair of small wings catching the candlelight, black eyes turned briefly toward the doorway.

A dark-haired young man with close, fine fur along his wrists folds a sheet of closely written paper and comes around the table. “Rowan Garvey? Rashid vel Amara—you are just in time; we had nearly decided the dinner bell had lost a guest.”

The tall woman beside the nearest chair has ember-red skin and swept black-red horns. “It does not ring for another minute,” she says. “Ashara vel Kothren. Sit before he files a petition about the delay.”

The vacant place beside her has a folded napkin, a shallow bowl, and a view of both the door and the first course waiting under its cover.

exchanges.player: I take the offered chair. "Rowan, yes. Apparently I should have some onion tart before anyone asks what a Garvey intends, so I hope the petitions can wait." I smile at them. "There was a letter from Mara Garvey in my room. Do either of you know who she was?"
exchanges.story:
You take the chair. A server sets a plate before you: a small round of onion tart, its browned top broken by threads of sharp white cheese, with a spoonful of dark greens beside it. The soup tureen begins its slow way around the table.

Rashid glances toward the common room and its ranks of painted Garveys. “Not personally. The brass plate by the fireplace calls her a resident trustee, and credits her with making this a Conclave residence.”

“Then she had decent priorities,” Ashara says. “Food first, inquiries second.”

Rashid settles into his own chair, the folded paper still at his elbow. “Was the letter merely a welcome, or did it say something you need help with?”

Around the table, the others resume the small movements of getting settled: a silver-haired woman turns a page in her menu; the white-haired woman by the window lifts her bowl to inspect the steam; the angel with the small wings reaches for the bread. The tart is still warm when the server pours the first ladle of soup.

exchanges.player: "Just a welcome, really. A very kind one. My parents died when I was young, and there is a lot about the family I never learned. Do you know whom I could ask about her tomorrow?" I try the tart, then turn back to both of them. "What are you hoping to study here? I am still getting my bearings."
exchanges.story:
The pastry gives way in crisp layers, the onions sweet beneath the salt of the cheese. Around it, the soup has begun to steam in everyone's bowls.

“Professor Gareth Stone is your best first call,” Rashid says. “He teaches human Covenant history, and he is usually in the library after noon; I came for treaty law and military policy, especially the things everyone calls neutral after a committee has made them expensive for the same people.”

Ashara takes a measured bite of tart before answering. “Strategy and Covenant law; the rankings tell you what you can do with a blade, and the law tells you who gets punished for having one.”

Rashid's mouth pulls briefly to one side at that, though he does not argue. The server passes the bread basket between them, and the white-haired woman by the window turns from the storm long enough to take a dark-crusted roll.

exchanges.player: "Thank you. I will try the library tomorrow." I settle into the meal, listening to the conversation and introducing myself when there is an opening. When I have finished eating, I say to Rashid and Ashara, "I could do with some air. Would either of you like a walk in the gardens? I kept looking at that light-bridge from my window."
exchanges.story:
The meal takes its time. Between the soup and the roast, introductions make their way around the table without ceremony. Ysolde Thornmantle gives her name with one eye still on the weather beyond the glass. Caelindra Vaeyn offers a formal nod over her menu. Seraphel Dawnquill sets her name into four plain, unrhymed lines; Thessaly Morrow says she is hungry before she says anything else; Aldric Verantus waits until the bread has reached him, then introduces himself with careful courtesy.

The talk moves from instructors to the eccentricities of Academy meals, then to the dueling rankings posted outside the grounds. Rashid complains that the list is updated in a hand designed to be illegible at a distance. Ashara says this may be because he insists on reading it while walking. At the far end of the table, Ysolde becomes unexpectedly absorbed in a disagreement about whether the storm has shifted north since last week, and Seraphel's brief verses draw a laugh from Thessaly.

By the time the last plates are cleared, the lamps have taken the place of the fading light outside. Rashid folds the paper at his elbow into quarters. “I would, but I promised Dena Arl I would look over a request with her before I take it to faculty.”

Ashara looks toward the garden doors. “I can spare one circuit of the gardens. The bridge is less impressive from ground level, but not much.”

Rashid tucks the paper inside his cuff and stands. Beyond the open doors, pale garden paths curve between the flowerbeds toward the wall, where the hard-light bridge rises over the storm.

exchanges.player: I wish Rashid luck with the request and go out with Ashara. I walk at an easy pace, pausing near the wall to look at the bridge and the storm beneath it. "I could watch that for ages. Where do you go when you get a whole evening to yourself?"
exchanges.story:
Rashid answers the wish with a brief lift of his hand before turning back toward the common room. Ashara waits only long enough to let him go, then takes the garden doors with you.

Outside, the air has a cool green scent from the beds along the path. Ashara's warmth travels beside you through the evening chill. At the wall, the bridge rises in a white, unwavering arc, broad enough for a carriage and somehow without visible support. Far below it, the storm turns over itself in slow blue flashes. The light catches the pale walls, the wet-looking leaves, the gold in Ashara's eyes.

“A whole evening is usually an administrative error,” she says. “When I find one, I take the dueling ground after dark—no crowd, no ranking clerk—and then I eat something hot enough to make everyone else complain.”

She rests one hand on the wall and looks along the bridge rather than down at the storm. “The grounds are better when nobody is there to mistake practice for a performance.”

exchanges.player: "I would be happy to complain about the food with you sometime. If you are eating after practice tomorrow, I would like to join you." I finish the circuit with her and thank her for the company. Back in my room, I check the primer for any first-morning instructions, then get ready for bed and turn in.
exchanges.story:
Ashara's gaze stays on the bridge for another moment. “Then you may have the chance. Meet me by the common-room hearth after the evening bell; if the bout runs late, eat without me.”

The rest of the circuit carries you past flowerbeds closed tight for the night and the old garden gate, its lower hinge furred with rust. At the doors, you thank her for the walk. Ashara gives a small inclination of her head. “Good night, Garvey.”

In your room, the primer's first-morning page is marked with an Academy seal and a neat block of instructions: breakfast begins at the seventh bell; new Conclave students report to the seminar room at the second bell after that, in Academy dress and carrying their identity seal. The morning holds an orientation with Chancellor Ashworth, a tour of the central halls, and appointments with the track advisers after midday.

The house has quieted by the time you set the primer aside. A last spill of lamp-glow reaches the framed letter, then the room goes dark around the made bed, the empty desk drawers, and the muted weather beyond the window.

exchanges.player: In the morning I get dressed as instructed and check that I have what the primer says to bring. I go down for breakfast at the seventh bell, then attend orientation and the tour. I pay attention to the way to the library and find out when my adviser appointment is, so I can look for Professor Stone without missing it.
exchanges.story:
At the seventh bell, the primer's list proves brief: Academy dress, identity seal, timetable, and something to write with. Breakfast is quieter than dinner had been. Schedules lie beside the plates; the conversation rises and falls around instructors, rooms, and whose assigned lecture has the earliest hour.

The Conclave seminar room holds fifteen chairs around its oval table, beneath the framed Accords in seven scripts. Chancellor Mordecai Ashworth conducts the orientation from a stack of neatly marked pages. He covers bridge permissions, library access, seminar conduct, and the expectation that first-years will meet with their advisers before choosing additional courses. His attention passes evenly around the room, though the old angel's eyes rest a moment longer on the Garvey signet when he reaches your name.

A registrar leads the tour through the quadrangle after the meeting: black demon stone warming under the morning sun, white angel marble bright at the chapel steps, living timber grown into the elven colonnade, and the low carved arches that open toward the dragon terraces. From the gardens, a covered passage leads directly to the library. Inside, lamp-oil and old paper meet the cool air from the iron spiral stair; open shelves fill both stories, while the restricted-history cabinet sits locked beneath its signed-access notice.

Just inside the library entrance, a faculty board gives Professor Gareth Stone's hours in a narrow north-gallery office: the second and third bells after midday. At the registry desk, your own appointment card reads: **Professor Kira vel Shaan, Practical Rhetoric — fourth bell after midday, Faculty Hall.** The walk between the library and Faculty Hall is marked on the tour map as less than ten minutes.

By the time the group disperses back into the quadrangle, the library doors stand open behind you, and there is a clear stretch of afternoon before the adviser appointment.

exchanges.player: I go to Professor Stone's office at the start of his posted hours and knock. "Professor Stone? Rowan Garvey. Rashid suggested I speak to you. There is a letter from Mara Garvey in my room, addressed to her great-nephew. I lost my parents young and know very little about this side of my family. Do you know whether she left any personal letters or papers I could read? I would like to know what she was like, and how we are related."
exchanges.story:
Professor Stone's office is narrow enough that the bookshelves seem to meet over the desk. A green-shaded lamp burns beside a card catalogue and a stack of student essays. At the knock, a chair scrapes across the floorboards.

The man who opens the door has silver threaded through his dark hair and ink on the heel of one hand. His eyes settle on the signet before they return to your face. “Come in, Mr. Garvey.”

He listens without interrupting, then pulls a thin drawer from the catalogue and scans a series of handwritten cards. “Mara was your grandfather's younger sister; her personal correspondence went to the Academy archives, though most originals require the chancellor's countersignature.”

Stone takes out one card and lays it on the desk between you. Beneath *GARVEY, MARA* are entries for household correspondence, garden accounts, and several letters marked open to Conclave students. “Some household letters are available to you, and I can show you how to request them; they will tell you more about her than the family chart will.”

The request shelf stands against the far wall, supplied with cream forms and a bottle of sand for drying ink. Through the open library doors, the north-gallery clock marks the beginning of the first office-hour bell.

exchanges.player: "Yes, please. I would like to start with the household letters I am allowed to see." I fill out the request with his guidance and take it where he directs. I explain that I have an appointment at the fourth bell, then settle at a reading table with something to write on, ready to read whatever can be brought out before I need to leave.
exchanges.story:
Stone turns the request form toward you and guides you through its narrow fields: collection, item class, consultation table, return time. “Mark only the open household material, not the general Garvey holdings. That will reach the desk today.”

At his direction, you take the completed form to the circulation desk. The librarian checks the adviser appointment card, stamps the request, and directs you to a long oak table beneath the north-gallery windows. “Bring the file back when you leave. It will wait for tomorrow; Professor Shaan will not.”

Your writing paper rests beside the blotter when an attendant arrives with a shallow green archive box. Inside are four pieces: two folded letters to Mrs. Pella, a household account, and a note to a carpenter about the garden gate. The first letter is dated *12 Rainmoot, 311 C.R.*

> Dear Mrs. Pella,
>
> Please have the garden gate repaired before Tuesday. It has begun to complain whenever it rains, and I refuse to let our guests think the house is falling down.
>
> We will be eleven at supper rather than eight. Put the onion tart on the sideboard if you want anyone else to have a slice; Sel says she dislikes cheese and has taken three portions already.
>
> Mara

The other letters remain folded in their sleeves, their dates and names visible through the thin paper. The north-gallery clock has not yet reached the next bell.

exchanges.player: The line about the cheese makes me smile. I read the second letter, the household account, and the carpenter's note, noting their names and dates. I ask the attendant whether I may make handwritten copies of the two letters to keep, and do so if permitted, keeping an eye on the clock.
exchanges.story:
The line about Sel and the tart draws the smile it seems designed to earn. The second letter is dated *3 Frostwane, 312 C.R.*, also addressed to Mrs. Pella.

> Dear Mrs. Pella,
>
> Keep the third place at Thursday's breakfast. Sel says she is leaving before dawn, which means she will appear at ten looking tragic and want toast.
>
> Ask the gardener to move the blue pots along the east wall. The roses have taken the path, and Aunt Bea will pretend not to notice until they catch her skirts.
>
> Mara

The household account is headed *Pella & Co., 15 Rainmoot, 311 C.R.* and records a carpenter's fee paid to Rill Fen for the lower garden hinge, eleven dinner covers, cheese, onions, lamp oil, and a crate of lemons. The carpenter's note, dated the following day and addressed to Master Fen, asks him to mend the gate rather than replace it, and to leave the latch low enough for young guests to use without help.

The attendant checks the open-consultation stamp on the request slip. “Handwritten copies of the letters are permitted at this table; use pencil, and keep the originals in their sleeves.”

You copy both letters onto the supplied paper, preserving Mara's dates, addressees, and the uneven turns of her handwriting. When the third bell after midday sounds, the attendant has taken back the green box and left the copies with you. The route to Faculty Hall remains clear on the tour map beside your notes, with the fourth bell still ahead.

exchanges.player: I stop by Stone's office to thank him and show him my copies. "May I ask one more thing before I go? Do you recognize Sel or Aunt Bea? I would like to know whether anyone mentioned here is still living." I put the copies carefully away afterward and leave enough time to reach Professor Shaan's appointment before the fourth bell.
exchanges.story:
Stone looks over the copied headings, then draws a slimmer index from the shelf behind his desk. His finger follows the Garvey entries down a page worn soft at the edges.

“Sel was Selene Garvey, Mara's younger sister; Aunt Bea was Beatrice Varo, their mother's sister.” He turns the index so the names and dates face you. “They both died long ago, and I do not find Pella or Fen in any current Academy registry.”

He marks the page with a strip of clean paper. “After your appointment, I can show you the reference if you would like to keep tracing the branch.”

You put the copied letters away with the primer. The north-gallery clock leaves enough of the third bell to cross the quadrangle, past the chapel steps and along the faculty offices without hurrying. Faculty Hall is quieter than the library; its thin doors bear small brass plates. At the end of the corridor, one reads **PROFESSOR KIRA VEL SHAAN — PRACTICAL RHETORIC**. The fourth bell has not yet sounded.

exchanges.player: At the fourth bell I knock and introduce myself to Professor Shaan, with my timetable ready. "I am interested in the history, but I am still very new to all of this. I do not even know whether I have any magic. What will be expected of me in Practical Rhetoric, and how should I go about choosing the rest of my courses?"
exchanges.story:
The fourth bell has barely finished when a woman's voice answers from inside. “Come in, Mr. Garvey.”

Professor Kira vel Shaan's office is warmer than the corridor. She sits behind a desk crowded with marked speech drafts, a copper tea pot, and a rack of slim practice blades used as rhetorical examples rather than weapons. Her swept-back horns are polished to a dull dark shine; her sleeves are rolled neatly above her wrists. She takes the timetable, reads it once, then sets it between you.

“Practical Rhetoric has no magic prerequisite: each week you will write and defend a brief, negotiate a live disagreement, and learn to say what you need without hiding the cost; I expect preparation, attention, and revision.”

She draws a line through the open elective spaces with a red pencil. “Take the required Conclave Institutions course, one history course, and an Arcana assessment before you decide magic has no place in your life; the remaining place should be something you would study even if no Council seat waited at the end of it.”

Kira turns the timetable so its blank choices face you again. On the shelf behind her, course catalogues stand in labeled rows: history, law, diplomacy, arcana, commerce, military theory. The advisor appointment has only just begun.

exchanges.player: "I would like to take Professor Stone's history course and arrange the Arcana assessment, then. For the last place, is there anything about growing things? I liked being out in the gardens last night. It would be good to learn how to care for a small patch of my own." I look through the relevant course information with her and ask how to book the assessment.
exchanges.story:
Kira pulls a green-bound catalogue from the shelf and opens it midway through. One entry is marked in red pencil: **Foundations of Living Grounds — soil, propagation, seasonal care, and managed enchantments; garden practicum twice weekly.** The course notes assign each student a small bed for the term and list no magical prerequisite.

“Foundations of Living Grounds fits. It is practical, taught in the gardens, and each student keeps a bed through the term.”

She enters Professor Stone's history course and the garden practicum on the timetable, then takes out a blue Arcana registry card. “For the assessment, bring this signed card to the south registry and choose an open slot; the screening is supervised, and it does not oblige you to take a magic course afterward.”

The card lists two openings: the second bell tomorrow afternoon or the sixth bell the following morning. Kira places it beside the completed course lines, along with a short reading list for Stone's course and a garden map marked with the practicum plots.

exchanges.player: I thank Professor Shaan and take the signed card to the south registry to book the second bell tomorrow afternoon. Back at the house, I lay the copied letters on my desk beside the primer and spend the rest of the free afternoon on Stone's reading list. When the evening bell sounds, I go to the common-room hearth to meet Ashara.
exchanges.story:
At the south registry, a clerk checks Kira's signature against the faculty seal and enters your name beneath the second-afternoon-bell assessment slot. The blue card comes back with a fresh stamp, the time written in a firm black hand.

Back at Garvey House, the copied letters lie beside the primer while Stone's reading list opens across the desk. The first selections move from a transcript of the Covenant's founding debates to later commentaries on bridge permissions and Council voting procedure. Their margins disagree sharply about what a phrase like *shared authority* was meant to demand, while the original speakers have left only their names, their clauses, and the objections entered into record.

By the evening bell, the windows have gone blue-grey over the gardens. The common-room hearth has been built up again, its fire throwing light across the old portraits and the empty study tables. Ashara is not there when you arrive.

A few minutes later, the garden door opens. She comes in with her hair still tied back from the grounds and a covered pot balanced on one hand, heat rising from it into the cooler room. “The bout finished on time. I secured stew before the Military cohort could discover it.”

She sets the pot on the hearthstone beside two bowls and a stack of flatbread.

exchanges.player: I fetch some water, sit with her, and take a cautious spoonful of stew. "Thank you for rescuing supper. I found some of my great-aunt's letters today. Mostly household fussing, but I had not expected that to mean so much." I tear off some flatbread. "How did your bout go?" I settle in to listen and enjoy an unhurried meal with her.
exchanges.story:
The stew is thick with lentils, roasted peppers, and a heat that arrives slowly behind the first spoonful. Ashara tears her own piece of flatbread and uses it to lift a strip of softened onion from the bowl.

“Household fussing is useful; it tells you who someone expected to have supper with.” She takes a drink of water. “My bout went to three passes, and I won the last by two touches after wasting the first trying to impress the judge.”

The fire settles with a low shift of wood. Outside the garden doors, the paths have emptied into darkness, but the bridge still throws a pale reflection across the window glass. Ashara takes another spoonful of stew, leaving the pot between you within easy reach.

exchanges.player: "Congratulations. I have my Arcana assessment tomorrow afternoon. I am curious, but rather nervous about it." I finish the meal at an easy pace, then help clear the bowls and pot. I thank Ashara for the evening and say goodnight. Upstairs, I put the stamped assessment card with my timetable where I can find it in the morning, then get ready for bed and go to sleep.
exchanges.story:
Ashara considers that over the rim of her bowl. “Mine was one proctor, a bowl of sand, and a list of responses. If yours has a ranking board, complain to me afterward; I will agree it was unnecessary.”

The meal winds down without haste. When the pot is empty, you help stack the bowls and carry it to the covered return tray at the dining-hall door. Ashara takes the flatbread basket from the hearthstone and puts its cloth back in place.

At the stairs, you thank her for the evening. “Sleep well, Garvey,” she says.

Upstairs, the stamped Arcana card goes with the timetable where the morning light will find both. The house has settled again by the time you put out the lamp. Beyond the window, the bridge's pale line remains above the storm until sleep takes the room.

exchanges.player: In the morning I have breakfast, check my timetable, and attend anything scheduled before midday. After lunch I take my stamped card and identity seal to the south registry, ask which room I need for the assessment, and make my way there about ten minutes before the second bell. I introduce myself and show the card.
exchanges.story:
The timetable gives the morning to the first Conclave Institutions seminar. Professor Windwhisper conducts it from the far side of the oval table, using a disputed bridge permit to trace the difference between a vote, a treaty obligation, and a courtesy. Her voice never rises, even when three students begin speaking at once. By midday, the case has been put aside without a winner and the next reading has been assigned.

After lunch, the south-registry clerk checks the stamp on the blue card and directs you to Assessment Room Three, along the lower colonnade beyond the Arcana lecture rooms. You reach its white-painted door with time to spare. The room beyond is spare and cool: a table set with a glass-cupped ember, a shallow dish of grey sand, a coil of copper thread, and a slate marked with a simple grid.

The examiner accepts the card and compares it with the Garvey signet. “Mr. Garvey, I am Examiner Sol. Sit wherever is comfortable; we begin with response to neutral foci.”

At Sol's direction, you place a hand in turn near the ember, the sand, the thread, and the slate. The ember burns steadily inside its glass. The sand remains level. The copper keeps its ordinary dull curve, and the grid stays blank while Sol notes each result.

When the second bell sounds beyond the colonnade, Sol closes the ledger. “You show no measurable resonance in the standard channels. I will record you as non-practical for now; you may study Arcana theory without restriction.”

exchanges.player: I sit quietly for a moment, surprised by the disappointment. "All right. Thank you. May I have a written copy of the result for my own records?" After collecting whatever paperwork there is, I take my leave and walk out to the gardens for some air. I unfold the practicum map and look for the student beds.
exchanges.story:
Sol takes out a two-part form and writes the result in a narrow, exact hand: **No measurable resonance in standard channels. No practical placement recommended.** A registry seal presses blue into the lower corner.

“Yes. Keep the original; registry receives the duplicate.”

The signed copy is dry by the time you leave the lower colonnade. In the gardens, afternoon air carries damp earth and the faint sweetness of the flowering hedges. The practicum map leads away from the main pale path, past a clipped yew wall, to a rectangular terrace of raised beds.

Each bed is edged in dark stone and marked with a small slate stake. Some hold newly turned soil, some close rows of seedlings, and some last season's dry stalks waiting to be cleared. A painted board at the gate reads **FOUNDATIONS OF LIVING GROUNDS — FIRST-YEAR PLOTS**. Beneath it, a list of student names has been pinned up, with the individual bed assignments still blank beside them.

Beyond the terrace, the garden wall catches the bridge's white light even in daylight. The map remains open in your hand, its practicum plots neatly numbered around the beds.

exchanges.player: I check the board and my timetable for the first garden practicum, then take a slow look around the beds, reading any labels beside the seedlings. Afterward I fold the map and head back to Garvey House. I look for Rashid in the common room; if he is there, I ask, "How did your meeting with Dena go?"
exchanges.story:
The practicum board and your timetable agree: **Foundations of Living Grounds** meets at the third bell after midday tomorrow. Until then, the terrace is quiet except for leaves moving against the stone edging.

You take the paths between the beds at an unhurried pace. Slate labels mark winter peas just pushing through the soil, lamp-mint with silver-furred leaves, bitterleaf kale, and a row of narrow blue-green seedlings labeled *river onions*. One bed has been cleared to bare dark earth; another is crossed with twine and a small note about testing its drainage after rain. At the far end of the terrace, a rain barrel feeds a set of clay channels running from plot to plot.

When you return to Garvey House, Rashid is in the common room with several sheets spread across a study table. He looks up from a page covered in crossed-out lines when you ask about Dena.

“She gave me useful corrections. We will make the request through attendance records and a safety plan, not one student's account; I am taking it to faculty review tomorrow.”

He taps the margin of the page with the end of his pen, then turns it over and reaches for a clean sheet.

exchanges.player: "I hope the review goes well. What are you asking them to change?" I listen to Rashid, then go upstairs to put the assessment report with my papers and collect my seminar reading. I bring it back to a nearby table in the common room and settle down to read there for a while.
exchanges.story:
Rashid squares the sheets beneath his hand. “Not an immediate reversal. I am asking for an inspection, the instructor's report, and two supervised evening blocks a week once the equipment is cleared; no student needs a private coach to keep training while the faculty decides what happened.”

He glances at the crossed-out draft. “If the injury came from negligence, the fix should answer that. If it did not, closing everyone out is still an answer of convenience.”

Upstairs, the Arcana report goes with the timetable and the copied Garvey letters. You return with Professor Windwhisper's seminar reading and take the nearest open study table in the common room. The assigned bridge-permit case unfolds through petitions, maintenance agreements, and a disagreement over whether a temporary restriction became a practical exclusion when it lasted through an entire season.

Rashid continues revising at the next table. The fire has burned low enough that the portraits' gilt frames catch more light than their faces, and the house holds the quiet sounds of pages turned, pen strokes, and someone moving upstairs.

exchanges.player:
My character: Rowan Garvey. A twenty-three-year-old human man with brown skin, unruly dark hair, and ink-stained fingers, wearing a carefully mended charcoal coat and the inherited Garvey signet. Newly arrived and unsure of Conclave customs. He grew up unaware of his heritage, lost his parents young, and does not know whether he has any magic.

Begin the story shortly before the welcome dinner, in my room at Garvey House. I play Rowan Garvey.
exchanges.story:
The last of the daylight lies blue across the window glass, turning the gardens below into pale paths and dark hedges. Beyond them, one of the hard-light bridges vanishes into the storm as neatly as a line drawn through wet ink.

Your room is orderly in the way a place prepared for a stranger must be: the bed smoothed flat, the mended charcoal coat given a hook beside the door, a row of clothes from the lawyers folded in the wardrobe. On the desk, the Academy primer rests beside a lamp with its wick already lit. The framed letter leaning against the wall has a narrow, slanting hand across its first line: *To my great-nephew.* The ink has faded brown at the edges.

Somewhere below, chairs scrape over a floor. A burst of conversation rises through the house, then settles again beneath the clink of plates being laid out.

A light knock comes at the door. When no one enters, a woman's voice says from the hall, "Dinner will be served shortly, Mr. Garvey. The dining hall is downstairs, past the common room."

The hall beyond your door carries the warmer smell of candlewax and roast herbs. At the far end, the stair curves down toward the voices.

exchanges.player: "Thank you. I'll be right down." I go to the dining hall, introduce myself, and take an empty seat. "Good evening. I'm Rowan." I help myself to dinner.
exchanges.story:
By the time you come down, the dining hall has gone bright with lamps. Candlelight runs along the varnished table and catches in seventeen waiting places, though only seven are occupied. A server draws back an empty chair on the garden side as you enter.

Your greeting reaches the table over the soft scrape of silverware. The wolf-blooded man nearest the bread rises first; his cuff is immaculate, his hands dark with fine fur. "Rashid vel Amara. Welcome to Garvey House."

The woman beside him has black-red horns swept back from a severe knot of hair. "Ashara vel Kothren," she says, and sits a little straighter as if the name is an introduction enough.

The rest follow without ceremony. White-haired Ysolde Thornmantle gives a small nod from across the table. Caelindra Vaeyn names herself while adjusting the fall of her silver hair. Thessaly Morrow offers hers with a brief, curious smile. Aldric Verantus greets you with grave warmth. The angel beside him, whose small white wings show between the folds of her gold-trimmed clothes, says,

"Seraphel Dawnquill.
May this house give you rest tonight."

Platters arrive: glazed root vegetables, saffron rice, a dark roast fragrant with rosemary, and a dish of green beans dressed in sharp citrus. You help yourself as the servers pass wine and chilled water along the table. Near Rashid's plate, a sheaf of papers has slipped loose from beneath his napkin; the top page bears the heading *Request for Supervised Court Access* before he tucks it back into place.

"They sent you a primer, I expect," Caelindra says, breaking a piece from the bread loaf. Her violet eyes settle on the Garvey signet. "Did the lawyers explain the Conclave, or merely teach you which hand to use for inheriting it?"

Ashara reaches for the salt. "That is unfair. Lawyers seldom explain anything that might prove useful."

exchanges.player: "Mostly titles. If I use the wrong spoon, I'm still on my own." I try some of the roast, then ask Caelindra, "What do you read when no one is going to examine you on it?"
exchanges.story:
The roast is tender under its dark glaze, smoky at the edges and brightened by the rosemary. Ashara looks at the orderly row of silver beside your plate.

"The wrong spoon is an Academy offense," she says. "They ring a bell and hang it over the gate."

"We do not," Aldric says.

"Not yet," Rashid adds, and takes a drink to hide the beginning of a smile.

Caelindra's knife stills against her plate at your question. For a moment she studies the candlewick between you rather than anyone at the table. "A collection called *The Minor Catastrophes*," she says at last. "Human verse. There is a magistrate, a missing parrot, and three invitations sent to the wrong people. It is very exact about embarrassment."

Thessaly turns her black gaze from the citrus beans to Caelindra. "That sounds useful."

"It is not useful," Caelindra says. The answer comes too quickly; she takes another bite, then looks back at you. "Do you read poetry, Rowan Garvey?"

exchanges.player: "Some, but I read more stories than poems. I've been working on a short one. Would you look at two pages after dinner?"
exchanges.story:
Caelindra sets down her glass with care. The candlelight catches along the edge of her silver hair as she considers you across the table.

"Two pages is a tolerable amount of risk," she says. "Bring them to the library after dinner. Leave me long enough to read them before you tell me what they mean."

Thessaly folds her hands beneath the tablecloth. "That has all the components of a bargain and none of the useful language."

"It is an arrangement," Caelindra says.

"Those are usually worse."

For the first time since you sat down, Caelindra's mouth threatens a smile before she takes another measured bite of dinner.

exchanges.player: I finish dinner, fetch the two pages from my room, and bring them to Caelindra in the library. The pages tell of a village cooper who accepts an order for six barrels, with half the price paid in advance. The delivery address turns out to belong to a man who has been dead for ten years. When she returns to her shop, three of the barrels are missing. That is where the pages end; I have not written who the customer is or how the barrels disappeared. I give her time to read, then ask, "Is there anything here you would want to read more of?"
exchanges.story:
By the time you return from your room, the dining hall has quieted behind you. The library smells of lamp oil and old leather. Its upper galleries disappear into shadow above the iron spiral stair, while pools of yellow light lie across the long reading tables.

Caelindra has taken a place near the windows, where the storm makes a dim, ceaseless motion beyond the glass. She accepts the two pages without ceremony and reads them standing at first, then sits when the cooper reaches the dead man's address.

She does not interrupt. The only sound for a while is the soft turn of paper and, somewhere in the stacks, wood settling in its joints. When she reaches the end, she reads the final paragraph once more. Her thumb holds the pages together at the corner.

"Yes," she says when you ask. "The cooper takes the advance. Sensible. Then half her work vanishes, and I want to know whether she goes after the money, the barrels, or the person who paid her."

She lays the pages flat on the table between you. "You stop at the right place. Why did you stop there?"

exchanges.player: "Because that's where I ran out of story for tonight. I haven't decided what happens next." I take back the pages. "Could I borrow The Minor Catastrophes when you've finished with it?"
exchanges.story:
Caelindra watches you gather the pages, then gives a small nod.

"That is a better reason than inventing an ending out of impatience," she says. "The book is in my room. I will bring it to breakfast tomorrow, and you may borrow it then."

She draws one finger along the grain of the table. "Do not annotate it."

exchanges.player: "Thank you. No marks." I say good night and leave her to her reading. Back in my room, I put away my story and read the primer for an hour before going to bed. In the morning I dress and go down to breakfast.
exchanges.story:
Caelindra acknowledges your good night with a nod and turns back to the lamp-lit page before her.

In your room, the primer takes up the next hour with its clean, official account of the Covenant: Council seats, bridge permissions, Academy tracks, and the forty years of war that made the treaties necessary. The human collapse occupies two restrained paragraphs under a heading about the plague. Article Nineteen receives more space, its penalties set out in careful legal language. By the time you put the book aside, the lamp has burned low.

Morning brings grey stormlight through the windows and the smell of coffee from below. When you come down dressed for the day, only a few places at the breakfast table are occupied. Caelindra sits near the gardens with a slim, blue-bound book beside the empty place across from her.

She moves it onto the table between you. "*The Minor Catastrophes.* The parrot arrives on page twelve. Do not begin there."

exchanges.player: I take the book. "No marks and no skipping. Thank you." I finish breakfast and attend my classes. After the last bell, I take the book to the library and spend an hour reading from the beginning.
exchanges.story:
Caelindra gives the book up without comment. Its blue cloth cover is softened at the corners from use.

Classes divide the day into bells, stairwells, and rooms full of other students learning how to sound certain. A morning survey traces the Council's votes through old border disputes; after midday, Practical Rhetoric has the class identify the concession hidden inside a polished argument. By the last bell, the quadrangle is washed in the blue-grey light of the storm.

You take *The Minor Catastrophes* to the library. The room is quieter than it was the night before, its lamps already burning against the early dark. At a table beneath the lower gallery, you begin at the first page.

The poems keep their disasters small and precise. A baker misdelivers a wedding cake to a funeral and spends six stanzas trying to reclaim the roses. A tenant writes increasingly formal notes to the mouse in her pantry. By page twelve, the missing parrot has learned a magistrate's private speech and repeats it from a pear tree while the man insists, with dwindling success, that the bird belongs to someone else.

An hour passes in the pool of lamplight. The book remains open before you, the next poem beginning on the facing page.

exchanges.player: At dinner I sit near Caelindra. "I read some of the book. The baker trying to recover the roses was my favourite, but I felt sorry for the magistrate. Having your private words repeated in public would be miserable."
exchanges.story:
Dinner has drawn most of the house back to the long table. You find a place near Caelindra while servers set down bowls of peppered lentils and flatbread still warm from the oven.

She listens to your verdict on the poems with her hands folded beside her plate. At the mention of the magistrate, one pointed ear shifts beneath her hair.

"The poem means you to feel sorry for him," she says. "A little. The parrot does not accuse him of anything. It merely repeats him."

She tears a piece of bread in two. "What I found less forgivable was that he left the cage outside because he expected a servant to notice it. The speech was private; the carelessness was not."

exchanges.player: "I'll finish it this week. I won't keep it from you long." For the next three days I attend classes, read in my free time, and finish The Minor Catastrophes. I return the book to Caelindra without any marks in it. On the third evening I come down to dinner as usual.
exchanges.story:
"See that you do," Caelindra says.

The next three days settle into the Academy's rhythm. Classes leave annotated handouts on your desk and new names in the margins of the primer; free hours find you back beneath the library lamps with *The Minor Catastrophes*. The book goes on finding trouble in overlooked places: a woman files a complaint against the rain for spoiling her laundry, a gardener mistakes a duke's private apology for a seed catalogue. Its last poem ends with a family dinner delayed by a missing key and never explains who has it.

When you return the blue-bound volume, Caelindra turns it once in her hands and opens it at random. The pages are clean.

"You finished it quickly," she says. "I hope the key disappointed you."

On the third evening, you come down to dinner as usual. The table is louder than it has been for the past few nights, with small conversations breaking and reforming over bowls of stew. Rashid has set a neat stack of papers beside the water carafe; several signatures already fill the first sheet.

He straightens the stack. "I am submitting the request for supervised court access tomorrow morning. If you train with the group and want your name on it, it is there."

exchanges.player: "Could the group practise in the gardens here while the court is closed? It's my house. I'm willing to let you, if that would help."
exchanges.story:
Rashid's hand remains on the stack of signatures. He considers the offer for a moment before answering.

"It is generous. Thank you," he says. "But I do not want a practice group that exists only because the human heir can spare a corner of his grounds. The people who attend need regular access without a favor owing."

Ashara reaches for her water. "The gardens could manage footwork and a practice blade. They are poor ground for anything involving a hard fall."

Rashid nods once. "If the other residents are willing, I will ask the group whether they want it as a temporary option. I am still filing the request."

exchanges.player: "I wasn't asking for a favour in return. Use it or don't, but I don't want every offer I make treated as a transaction."
exchanges.story:
Rashid's expression settles into careful courtesy.

"I did not say you named a price," he says. "A favor can be freely given and still leave one person deciding whether everyone else gets a place to train. That is what I am trying to change."

He shifts the petition stack square with the edge of the table. "I should have said it without making you sound calculating."

exchanges.player: "All right. The offer stands as a temporary stopgap." I turn toward the other residents at the table. "Would an hour of footwork in the gardens on two evenings next week bother any of you? No sparring or hard falls."
exchanges.story:
Ashara answers first. "No objection. The eastern path has room for drills if you stay off the gravel."

Ysolde turns her glass slowly between both hands. "The wall there also keeps out most of the wind."

"Two hours beneath the garden wall\nwill not disturb me," Seraphel says.

Caelindra glances toward the dark windows. "Nor me. Keep clear of the moonflower beds."

"I have no objection," Aldric says. "The restriction was a precaution, not a command against learning."

Rashid looks around the table as the answers settle. "Then I will ask the group which two evenings work and bring the times here before I confirm them. The petition still goes in tomorrow."

exchanges.player: "Let me know what they say." I leave Rashid to arrange things with the group and spend the next few days on classes, reading, and walks in the gardens. I keep coming down to the shared meals.
exchanges.story:
The next few days acquire a rhythm. Classes fill the mornings and afternoons; in the gaps, you read where you can find a quiet table. Your walks take you along the garden walls, where the sheltered air holds the scent of wet stone and flowering vines while lightning moves slowly below the plateau. At meals, the long table makes room for ordinary complaints about assignments, jokes that do not need repeating, and the practical business of passing dishes.

On the fourth evening, Rashid arrives at dinner with the petition stack gone from under his arm. He waits until the servers have set down the soup before speaking to the table.

"The group chose Tuesday and Thursday, one hour after the last bell, on the eastern path," he says. "Six people can make both evenings, and everyone understands there will be no sparring. I submitted the request this morning. We will see whether the Academy answers before then."

exchanges.player: "Did something delay the request? I thought it was going in the morning after we discussed the gardens."
exchanges.story:
Rashid sets his spoon down.

"Yes," he says. "I did not tell the table that I was delaying it. Some of the people who wanted the access request signed did not want their accounts of the injury made public. I needed a way to ask for both without using anyone's name as evidence."

He looks briefly at the space beside the soup bowl, then back at you. "I should have said that sooner."

exchanges.player: "That makes sense. I'm glad you checked with them." On Tuesday, an hour after the last bell, I take my notebook to a garden bench away from the eastern path. I stay for the practice session, quietly watching without joining the drills, until the hour is over.
exchanges.story:
Rashid gives a brief nod across the dinner table. "So am I."

On Tuesday, the eastern garden path is already marked with small chalk lines by the time you take a bench beyond the low wall. Your notebook rests beside you while the practice group gathers in twos and threes, shedding satchels and jackets onto the stone.

Rashid begins with foot placement. He walks the length of the path once, heel and toe falling between the chalk marks, then has them repeat the pattern in silence. A pair of students keep drifting toward the gravel and are sent back to begin again. When they move on to turns, he makes them stop before the pivot becomes a stumble: step, turn, recover, reset.

The hour finds its own pace. There are stretches of counted movement, short breaks for water, a complaint about a torn shoe, and the dry scrape of practice blades drawn only to measure distance. No one strikes. Near the end, Rashid has them work through the same sequence without the chalk lines, each person choosing where to stop before the flowerbeds.

When the Academy bell carries over from the quadrangle, he calls the session finished. The group collects its things and leaves the eastern path as it found it, except for a few pale chalk smudges on the stone.

exchanges.player: "Caelindra, do you remember where and when we arranged to meet for my reading?"
exchanges.story:
The dining hall still holds its pre-dinner hush: candlelight catches in the varnish of the long table, and servers move quietly between the high-backed chairs. At your question, Caelindra lifts her eyes from the place card before her.

“Friday after dinner, in the common room,” she says. “You reserved it, and I said I intended to come. Has that changed?”

Seraphel’s small wing brushes the back of her chair. “Rashid told me this afternoon
that your reading had moved.
He named neither place nor hour.”

exchanges.player: "Yes. The common room needs floor repairs. The porter moved the reservation to the west terrace at noon on Sunday, and I agreed. I'm sorry I left you with the old arrangement. Does the new time still work for you?"
exchanges.story:
Caelindra lets the apology settle between the candle flames. One pointed ear turns slightly toward the door as a pair of servers pass behind the chairs, their covered dishes sending up a thread of rosemary and butter.

“Sunday at noon works for me,” she says. “You should have told us sooner, but floor repairs are not a personal affront. I will come to the west terrace.”

Seraphel folds her hands beside her plate. “Sunday at noon
will still receive me.
Thank you for telling us.”
